Z:\claude-sota\.claude\rules\parallel-session-worktree-isolation.md:107:   - **(c) Lockfile + O_CREAT|O_APPEND atomic-write for SHARED JSONL append**: open the JSONL log with `os.open(path, os.O_CREAT | os.O_APPEND | os.O_WRONLY, mode)` where `mode` defaults to `0o600` (owner-only — per Round-5b T3 round-3 NEEDS-ATTENTION conf=0.78 NEW-CLASS trust-boundary finding on commit `c2b5dee`: `0o644` was world-readable and leaked audit-trail content (agent prompts, PIDs, verdict cite paths, `agent_id` UUIDs, T1/T2/T3 verdict bodies) on multi-user hosts. Callers MAY opt-in to `0o640` group-readable for shared-CI cases via explicit `mode=` argument + documented umask interaction (e.g., `umask 0o027` for CI runner) — `0o644` is REJECTED as default for any audit-trail JSONL). **Migration semantic for legacy files** *(Round-7 amendment per T3 round-4 NEEDS-ATTENTION conf=0.91 NEW-CLASS finding on commit `df37fb1`; closes non-migrating gap caught by codex GPT-5.5 BRIDGE-MODE — POSIX `os.open` applies `mode` ONLY when `O_CREAT` actually CREATES the file)*: pre-existing files at `0o644` (created under Round-3-through-5 mandates pre-Round-6) RETAIN their world-readable perms after open, leaving the audit-trail leak intact unless coerced. After every `os.open`, the caller MUST: (i) read `current_mode = stat.S_IMODE(os.fstat(fd).st_mode)`; (ii) if `current_mode != mode` AND the file is owned by caller-uid, call `os.fchmod(fd, mode)` to coerce existing file to the mode invariant; (iii) if `os.fchmod` raises (`PermissionError` due to read-only mount, alien owner, ACL conflict on Windows NTFS, etc.), FAIL CLOSED — propagate the exception rather than proceeding with non-conforming perms (the audit-trail invariant is enforced everywhere or fails loudly). Document in commit body for any consumer applying this rule: one-time migration shell command `find .claude/state -name '*.jsonl' -perm /044 -exec chmod 0600 {} +` (POSIX) OR `Get-ChildItem -Path .claude/state -Filter *.jsonl -Recurse | Where-Object { ($_ | Get-Acl).AccessToString -match 'Everyone Allow Read' } | ForEach-Object { icacls $_.FullName /inheritance:r /grant ${env:USERNAME}:F }` (Windows) for legacy `mcp_health.jsonl` / `subagent_transcripts.jsonl` / `codex_postcommit_reviews.jsonl` / `subagent_start.jsonl` / `worktree_lifecycle_audit.jsonl` files created at `0o644` per pre-Round-6 mandates. The `O_CREAT` flag ensures a missing log auto-creates rather than failing the first writer; **if `os.open` raises (read-only mount, permission denied, disk full), the exception MUST propagate — do not catch-and-ignore** (per Round-5 F-1 silent-failure finding). Take an **exclusive advisory lock** (`fcntl.flock(fd, LOCK_EX)` on POSIX / `msvcrt.locking` on Windows); **if neither primitive is available, or if the platform does not enforce advisory locks (e.g., NFS without NLM support), FAIL CLOSED — raise rather than proceeding without a lock** (per Round-5 F-2 NFS-silent-succeed finding). **Windows separate-lockfile mechanism** *(Round-7c per T3 round-7b NEEDS-ATTENTION conf=0.78 NEW-CLASS finding on commit `48c49fb` caught by codex GPT-5.5 BRIDGE-MODE)*: `msvcrt.locking` locks `nbytes` from CURRENT file-pointer position, NOT the whole file like POSIX `fcntl.flock`. Under O_APPEND the JSONL fd's pointer moves on each write, breaking lock-release symmetry (LK_UNLCK at the new pointer would find no lock at the byte LK_LOCK was issued for). Round-7b workaround (shipped at `scripts/_atomic_jsonl_append.py:_acquire_lock(fd, path)` commit `48c49fb`): open separate `<jsonl-path>.lock` file with 1-byte placeholder + lock byte 0 of the LOCKFILE (no writes to lockfile means file pointer stays at byte 0). Module returns `lock_fd` for Windows callers to release; `None` for POSIX. **Lock-protocol rollout constraint** *(Round-7c per same T3 finding)*: when the lock protocol bumps (direct-jsonl-fd → separate-lockfile-v1, or separate-lockfile-v1 → separate-lockfile-v2-versioned), enforce single-version deployment for the entire concurrent-writer cohort. Old + new code locking DIFFERENT lock domains do NOT mutually exclude — concurrent writers can race even though each ALONE acquires its lock correctly. Mitigations (pick ONE before any concurrent rollout): **(i) transitional dual-lock**: acquire both old AND new protocol locks in series during the transition window; **(ii) runtime version-marker**: write protocol-version byte to lockfile + fail-closed on read-version-mismatch (FORWARD-REF for v2 lock protocol bump); **(iii) single-version cohort barrier**: coordinate cohort upgrade via deployment system before any new-version runs. Currently sss has ZERO consumers of `_atomic_jsonl_append.py` (FORWARD-REF wire-up Ships 2-5 pending per `tmp/wave22-orchestrator-salvage-jsonl-mode-bits-audit-2026-05-05.md`), so the version-skew window is THEORETICAL until first hook migrates to use the module. Future protocol bumps MUST honor one of (i)/(ii)/(iii). HOLD the lock across BOTH (a) JSON-encoding the record AND (b) the single low-level `os.write(fd, encoded_bytes)` — never use buffered text writes (`f.write(json.dumps(rec) + "\n")` via Python file objects can split into multiple writes). **If JSON encoding raises (`UnicodeEncodeError`, non-serializable type), release the lock and propagate the exception — do not silently drop the record** (per Round-5 F-3 silent-record-drop finding). For records where **`len(encoded_bytes)` — the byte count AFTER JSON encoding, NOT the key count of the dict —** exceeds the platform atomic-write bound (≤PIPE_BUF 4KB POSIX; ≤512 bytes for Windows or treat the lock as the sole correctness boundary), reject the record OR shard via option (b) filename-namespace; do NOT silently truncate (per Round-5 F-5 measurement-target finding). After the write, `os.fsync(fd)` if durability is part of the contract (audit-trail JSONL needs fsync; ephemeral telemetry may skip); **if `os.fsync` raises (`EIO`, `ENOSPC`), propagate the exception — do not silently ignore a durability failure when durability is contracted** (per Round-5 F-4 fsync-failure finding). Use for SHARED JSONL log targets (`mcp_health.jsonl`, `subagent_transcripts.jsonl`, `codex_postcommit_reviews.jsonl` class) where consumers expect interleaved appends from multiple writers and unified-view semantics are required.

1:---
2:name: ccpm
3:description: "CCPM - spec-driven project management: PRD → Epic → GitHub Issues → parallel agents → shipped code. Use this skill for anything in the software delivery lifecycle: writing a PRD ('write a PRD for X', 'let's plan X', 'scope this out'), parsing a PRD into an epic, decomposing an epic into tasks, syncing to GitHub ('sync the X epic', 'push tasks to github'), starting work on an issue ('start working on issue N', 'let's work on issue N'), analyzing parallel work streams, running standups ('standup', 'run the standup'), checking status ('what's next', 'what's blocked', 'what are we working on'), closing issues, or merging an epic. Use ccpm any time the user is talking about shipping a feature, managing work, or tracking progress — even if they don't say 'ccpm' or 'PRD'. Do NOT use for: debugging code, writing tests, reviewing PRs, or raw GitHub issue/PR operations with no delivery context."
4:---
5:
6:# CCPM - Claude Code Project Manager
7:
8:A spec-driven development workflow: PRD → Epic → GitHub Issues → Parallel Agents → Shipped Code.
9:
10:## Core Philosophy
11:
12:Requirements live in files, not heads. Every feature starts as a PRD, becomes a technical epic, decomposes into GitHub issues, and gets executed by parallel agents with full traceability.
13:
14:## File Conventions
15:
16:Before doing anything, read `references/conventions.md` for path standards, frontmatter schemas, and GitHub operation rules. These apply to all phases.
17:
18:## The Five Phases
19:
20:### 1. Plan — Capture requirements
21:**When**: User wants to define a new feature, product requirement, or scope of work.
22:**Read**: `references/plan.md`
23:**Covers**: Writing PRDs through guided brainstorming, converting PRDs to technical epics.
24:
25:### 2. Structure — Break it down
26:**When**: An epic exists and needs to be decomposed into concrete tasks.
27:**Read**: `references/structure.md`
28:**Covers**: Epic decomposition into numbered task files with dependencies and parallelization.
29:
30:### 3. Sync — Push to GitHub
31:**When**: Local epic/tasks need to become GitHub issues, progress needs to be posted as comments, or a bug is found and needs a linked issue created.
32:**Read**: `references/sync.md`
33:**Covers**: Epic sync (epic + tasks → GitHub issues), issue sync (progress comments), closing issues/epics, bug reporting against completed issues.
34:
35:### 4. Execute — Start building
36:**When**: User wants to start working on one or more GitHub issues with parallel agents.
37:**Read**: `references/execute.md`
38:**Covers**: Issue analysis (parallel work stream identification), launching parallel agents, coordinating worktrees.
39:
40:### 5. Track — Know where things stand
41:**When**: User asks for status, standup report, what's blocked, what's next, or needs to validate state.
42:**Read**: `references/track.md`
43:**Covers**: Status, standup, search, in-progress, next priority, blocked items, validation.
44:
45:---
46:
47:## Script-First Rule
48:
49:For deterministic operations — anything that reads and reports without needing reasoning — always run the bash script directly rather than doing the work manually:
50:
51:| What the user wants | Script to run |
52:|---|---|
53:| Project status | `bash references/scripts/status.sh` |
54:| Standup report | `bash references/scripts/standup.sh` |
55:| List all epics | `bash references/scripts/epic-list.sh` |
56:| Show epic details | `bash references/scripts/epic-show.sh <name>` |
57:| Epic status | `bash references/scripts/epic-status.sh <name>` |
58:| List PRDs | `bash references/scripts/prd-list.sh` |
59:| PRD status | `bash references/scripts/prd-status.sh` |
60:| Search issues/tasks | `bash references/scripts/search.sh <query>` |
61:| What's in progress | `bash references/scripts/in-progress.sh` |
62:| What's next | `bash references/scripts/next.sh` |
63:| What's blocked | `bash references/scripts/blocked.sh` |
64:| Validate project state | `bash references/scripts/validate.sh` |
65:
66:Use the LLM for work that requires reasoning: writing PRDs, analyzing parallelism, launching agents, synthesizing updates.
67:

54:## Background
55:
56:Every team struggles with the same problems:
57:- **Context evaporates** between sessions, forcing constant re-discovery
58:- **Parallel work creates conflicts** when multiple agents touch the same code
59:- **Requirements drift** as verbal decisions override written specs
60:- **Progress becomes invisible** until the very end
61:
62:CCPM solves all of that.
63:

66:## The Workflow
67:
68:```mermaid
69:graph LR
70:    A[PRD Creation] --> B[Epic Planning]
71:    B --> C[Task Decomposition]
72:    C --> D[GitHub Sync]
73:    D --> E[Parallel Execution]
74:```

77:

79:"I want to build a notification system — where do we start?"

83:→ Parallelizable task files with dependencies
84:

97:## What Makes This Different
98:
99:| Traditional AI Development | CCPM |
100:|---|---|
101:| Context lost between sessions | **Persistent context** across all work |
102:| One agent, one task | **Parallel agents** on independent streams |
103:| Vibe coding from memory | **Spec-driven** with full traceability |
104:| Progress hidden in chat logs | **Transparent audit trail** in GitHub |
105:| Scattered status updates | **Structured standup, blocked, next** |

107:---
108:
109:## Why GitHub Issues
110:
111:Most AI coding workflows operate in isolation — a single session with no shared state. CCPM uses GitHub Issues as the source of truth, which unlocks something fundamentally different:
112:
113:**Team collaboration** — multiple agents (or humans) work on the same project simultaneously. Progress is visible in real-time through issue comments.
114:
115:**Seamless handoffs** — an agent can start a task, a human can finish it, or vice versa. No "what did the AI do?" meetings.
116:
117:**Single source of truth** — no separate databases or project management tools. Issue state is project state. Comments are the audit trail.
118:
119:**Works with what you have** — no dependency on GitHub Projects. Integrates with existing labels, milestones, and PR workflows.
120:
121:---
122:
123:## Core Principle: No Vibe Coding
124:
125:> **Every line of code must trace back to a specification.**
126:
127:CCPM enforces a strict 5-phase discipline:
128:
129:1. **🧠 Brainstorm** — think deeper than comfortable
130:2. **📝 Document** — write specs that leave nothing to interpretation
131:3. **📐 Plan** — architect with explicit technical decisions
132:4. **⚡ Execute** — build exactly what was specified
133:5. **📊 Track** — maintain transparent progress at every step
134:
135:No shortcuts. No assumptions. No regrets.
136:
137:---
138:
139:## The Parallel Execution System
140:
141:### Issues Aren't Atomic
142:
143:Traditional thinking: **one issue = one agent = one task**
144:
145:Reality: a single "Implement user authentication" issue is actually:
146:
147:- **Agent 1**: Database tables and migrations
148:- **Agent 2**: Service layer and business logic
149:- **Agent 3**: API endpoints and middleware
150:- **Agent 4**: UI components and forms
151:- **Agent 5**: Test suites and documentation
152:
153:All running **simultaneously** in the same worktree.
154:
155:### The Math of Velocity
156:
157:| Approach | Agents working | Wall time |
158:|---|---|---|
159:| Traditional (serial) | 1 | 5x |
160:| CCPM (parallel streams) | 5 | 1x |
161:
162:### Context Stays Clean
163:
164:Each agent handles its own context in isolation. Your main conversation becomes the conductor — it never drowns in implementation details. Agents read from `.claude/epics/` and commit progress back through Git.
165:

168:## Key Features & Benefits
169:
170:**🧠 Context preservation** — project state lives in files, not in your head or chat history. Start a session anywhere, any time.
171:
172:**⚡ Parallel execution** — tasks marked `parallel: true` run concurrently across multiple agents without conflicts.
173:
174:**🔗 GitHub native** — works with tools your team already uses. No dependency on the Projects API.
175:
176:**📊 Full traceability** — every decision documented. PRD → Epic → Task → Issue → Code → Commit.
177:
178:**🤖 Deterministic ops run as scripts** — status, standup, search, validate all run as bash scripts: fast, consistent, no LLM token cost.
179:
180:**🌐 Harness-agnostic** — follows the [agentskills.io](https://agentskills.io) open standard. Works with Factory, Claude Code, Amp, OpenCode, Codex, Cursor, and more.

239:
240:## Workflow Phases
241:
242:### 1. Plan — Capture requirements
243:
244:```
245:"I want to build a notification system — push, email, and in-app"
246:```
247:
248:CCPM conducts guided brainstorming before writing anything. It asks about the problem, users, success criteria, constraints, and what's out of scope — then creates a structured PRD at `.claude/prds/<name>.md`.
249:
250:When ready: "parse the notification-system PRD" → produces a technical epic at `.claude/epics/notification-system/epic.md` with architecture decisions, technical approach, and task preview.
251:
252:### 2. Structure — Break it down
253:
254:```
255:"break down the notification-system epic into tasks"
256:```
257:
258:Each task gets a file with acceptance criteria, effort estimate, `depends_on`, `parallel`, and `conflicts_with` metadata. Tasks are intelligently batched for parallel creation. ≤10 tasks per epic by default.
259:
260:### 3. Sync — Push to GitHub
261:
262:```
263:"sync the notification-system epic to GitHub"
264:```
265:
266:Creates an epic issue, creates sub-issues for each task, renames local files to match GitHub issue numbers, sets up a dedicated worktree (`../epic-notification-system/`), and creates a mapping file for reference.
267:
268:### 4. Execute — Start building
269:
270:```
271:"start working on issue 42"
272:```
273:
274:Analyzes the issue for independent work streams, launches parallel agents scoped to their own files, and sets up progress tracking. Each agent commits with `Issue #N: description` and coordinates through Git.
275:
276:### 5. Track — Know where things stand
277:
278:```
279:"standup" / "what's blocked" / "what's next"
280:```
281:
282:All tracking operations run as bash scripts — instant output, no LLM overhead. The scripts scan `.claude/epics/` and report what's in progress, what's next, and what's blocked.
283:

286:## Skill Structure
287:
288:```
289:skill/ccpm/
290:├── SKILL.md                  # Entry point — detects intent, routes to reference
291:└── references/
292:    ├── plan.md               # PRD writing + parsing to epic
293:    ├── structure.md          # Epic decomposition into tasks
294:    ├── sync.md               # GitHub sync, progress comments, close, merge
295:    ├── execute.md            # Issue analysis + parallel agent launch
296:    ├── track.md              # Status, standup, search, next, blocked
297:    ├── conventions.md        # File formats, frontmatter schemas, git rules
298:    └── scripts/              # Bash scripts for deterministic operations
299:        ├── status.sh
300:        ├── standup.sh
301:        ├── epic-list.sh
302:        ├── search.sh
303:        └── ...               # 14 scripts total
304:```
305:
306:Your project files live in `.claude/` in your project root:
307:
308:```
309:.claude/
310:├── prds/                     # Product requirement documents
311:├── epics/
312:│   └── <feature>/
313:│       ├── epic.md           # Technical epic
314:│       ├── <N>.md            # Task files (named by GitHub issue number after sync)
315:│       ├── <N>-analysis.md   # Parallel work stream analysis
316:│       └── updates/          # Agent progress tracking
317:└── (archived epics)
318:```
319:
320:Files are the source of truth — plain markdown that lives in your repo, no external services.

403:
404:## Technical Notes
405:
406:**GitHub integration** — uses `gh-sub-issue` extension for proper parent-child relationships. Falls back to task lists if not installed. Install with: `gh extension install yahsan2/gh-sub-issue`
407:
408:**File naming** — tasks start as `001.md`, `002.md` during decomposition. After GitHub sync, renamed to `{issue-id}.md` (e.g. `1234.md`). Issue #1234 = file `1234.md`.
409:
410:**Design decisions** — intentionally avoids GitHub Projects API complexity. All operations work on local files first for speed. GitHub sync is explicit and controlled. Worktrees provide clean git isolation for parallel work.
411:
412:**Looking for v1?** — The original `/pm:*` Claude Code slash command system is preserved on the [`v1` branch](https://github.com/automazeio/ccpm/tree/v1).

1:# Execute — Start Building with Parallel Agents
2:
3:This phase covers analyzing GitHub issues for parallel work streams and launching agents to execute them.
4:
5:---
6:
7:## Issue Analysis
8:
9:**Trigger**: User wants to understand how to parallelize work on an issue before starting.
10:
11:### Preflight
12:- Find the local task file: check `.claude/epics/*/<N>.md` first, then search for `github:.*issues/<N>` in frontmatter.
13:- If not found: "❌ No local task for issue #<N>. Run a sync first."
14:
15:### Process
16:
17:Get issue details: `gh issue view <N> --json title,body,labels`
18:
19:Read the local task file fully. Identify independent work streams by asking:
20:- Which files will be created/modified?
21:- Which changes can happen simultaneously without conflict?
22:- What are the dependencies between changes?
23:
24:**Common stream patterns:**
25:- Database Layer: schema, migrations, models
26:- Service Layer: business logic, data access
27:- API Layer: endpoints, validation, middleware
28:- UI Layer: components, pages, styles
29:- Test Layer: unit tests, integration tests
30:
31:Create `.claude/epics/<epic_name>/<N>-analysis.md`:
32:
33:```markdown
34:---
35:issue: <N>
36:title: <title>
37:analyzed: <run: date -u +"%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ">
38:estimated_hours: <total>
39:parallelization_factor: <1.0-5.0>
40:---
41:
42:# Parallel Work Analysis: Issue #<N>
43:
44:## Overview
45:
46:## Parallel Streams
47:
48:### Stream A: <Name>
49:**Scope**: 
50:**Files**: 
51:**Can Start**: immediately
52:**Estimated Hours**: 
53:**Dependencies**: none
54:
55:### Stream B: <Name>
56:**Scope**: 
57:**Files**: 
58:**Can Start**: after Stream A
59:**Dependencies**: Stream A
60:
61:## Coordination Points
62:### Shared Files
63:### Sequential Requirements
64:
65:## Conflict Risk Assessment
66:
67:## Parallelization Strategy
68:
69:## Expected Timeline
70:- With parallel execution: <max_stream_hours>h wall time
71:- Without: <sum_all_hours>h
72:- Efficiency gain: <pct>%
73:```
74:
75:**Output**: "✅ Analysis complete for issue #<N> — N parallel streams identified. Ready to start? Say: start issue <N>"
76:
77:---
78:
79:## Starting an Issue
80:
81:**Trigger**: User wants to begin work on a specific GitHub issue.
82:
83:### Preflight
84:1. Verify issue exists and is open: `gh issue view <N> --json state,title,labels,body`
85:2. Find local task file (as above).
86:3. Check for analysis file: `.claude/epics/*/<N>-analysis.md` — if missing, run analysis first (or do both in sequence: analyze then start).
87:4. Verify epic worktree exists: `git worktree list | grep "epic-<name>"` — if not: "❌ No worktree. Sync the epic first."
88:
89:### Process
90:
91:**Step 1 — Read the analysis**, identify which streams can start immediately vs. which have dependencies.
92:
93:**Step 2 — Create progress tracking:**
94:```bash
95:mkdir -p .claude/epics/<epic>/updates/<N>
96:current_date=$(date -u +"%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ")
97:```
98:
99:Create `.claude/epics/<epic>/updates/<N>/stream-<X>.md` for each stream:
100:```markdown
101:---
102:issue: <N>
103:stream: <stream_name>
104:started: <datetime>
105:status: in_progress
106:---
107:## Scope
108:## Progress
109:- Starting implementation
110:```
111:
112:**Step 3 — Launch parallel agents** for each stream that can start immediately:
113:
114:```yaml
115:Task:
116:  description: "Issue #<N> Stream <X>"
117:  subagent_type: "general-purpose"
118:  prompt: |
119:    You are working on Issue #<N> in the epic worktree at: ../epic-<name>/
120:    
121:    Your stream: <stream_name>
122:    Your scope — files to modify: <file_patterns>
123:    Work to complete: <stream_description>
124:    
125:    Instructions:
126:    1. Read full task from: .claude/epics/<epic>/<N>.md
127:    2. Read analysis from: .claude/epics/<epic>/<N>-analysis.md
128:    3. Work ONLY in your assigned files
129:    4. Commit frequently: "Issue #<N>: <specific change>"
130:    5. Update progress in: .claude/epics/<epic>/updates/<N>/stream-<X>.md
131:    6. If you need to touch files outside your scope, note it in your progress file and wait
132:    7. Never use --force on git operations
133:    
134:    Complete your stream's work and mark status: completed when done.
135:```
136:
137:Streams with unmet dependencies are queued — launch them as their dependencies complete.
138:
139:**Step 4 — Assign on GitHub:**
140:```bash
141:gh issue edit <N> --add-assignee @me --add-label "in-progress"
142:```
143:
144:**Step 5 — Create execution status file** at `.claude/epics/<epic>/updates/<N>/execution.md`:
145:```markdown
146:## Active Streams
147:- Stream A: <name> — Started <time>
148:- Stream B: <name> — Started <time>
149:
150:## Queued
151:- Stream C: <name> — Waiting on Stream A
152:
153:## Completed
154:(none yet)
155:```
156:
157:**Output:**
158:```
159:✅ Started work on issue #<N>
160:
161:Launched N agents:
162:  Stream A: <name> ✓ Started
163:  Stream B: <name> ✓ Started
164:  Stream C: <name> ⏸ Waiting (depends on A)
165:
166:Monitor: check progress in .claude/epics/<epic>/updates/<N>/
167:Sync updates: "sync issue <N>"
168:```
169:
170:---
171:
172:## Starting a Full Epic
173:
174:**Trigger**: User wants to launch parallel agents across all ready issues in an epic at once.
175:
176:### Preflight
177:- Verify `.claude/epics/<name>/epic.md` exists and has a `github:` field (i.e., it's been synced).
178:- Check for uncommitted changes: `git status --porcelain` — block if dirty.
179:- Verify epic branch exists: `git branch -a | grep "epic/<name>"`
180:
181:### Process
182:
183:**Step 1 — Read all task files** in `.claude/epics/<name>/`. Parse frontmatter for `status`, `depends_on`, `parallel`.
184:
185:**Step 2 — Categorize tasks:**
186:- Ready: status=open, no unmet depends_on
187:- Blocked: has unmet depends_on
188:- In Progress: already has an execution file
189:- Complete: status=closed
190:
191:**Step 3 — Analyze any ready tasks** that don't have an analysis file yet (run issue analysis inline).
192:
193:**Step 4 — Launch agents** for all ready tasks following the same per-issue agent launch pattern above.
194:
195:**Step 5 — Create/update** `.claude/epics/<name>/execution-status.md` with all active agents and queued issues.
196:
197:**Step 6 — As agents complete**, check if blocked issues are now unblocked and launch those agents.
198:
199:---
200:
201:## Agent Coordination Rules
202:
203:When multiple agents work in the same worktree simultaneously:
204:
205:- Each agent works only on files in its assigned stream scope.
206:- Agents commit frequently with `Issue #<N>: <description>` format.
207:- Before modifying a shared file, check `git status <file>` — if another agent has it modified, wait and pull first.
208:- Agents sync via commits: `git pull --rebase origin epic/<name>` before starting new file work.
209:- Conflicts are never auto-resolved — agents report them and pause.
210:- No `--force` flags ever.
211:
212:Shared files that commonly need coordination (types, config, package.json) should be handled by one designated stream; others pull after that commit.

7:## Repository Safety Check
8:
9:**Always run this before any GitHub write operation:**
10:
11:```bash
12:remote_url=$(git remote get-url origin 2>/dev/null || echo "")
13:if [[ "$remote_url" == *"automazeio/ccpm"* ]]; then
14:  echo "❌ Cannot sync to the CCPM template repository."
15:  echo "Update remote: git remote set-url origin https://github.com/YOUR/REPO.git"
16:  exit 1
17:fi
18:REPO=$(echo "$remote_url" | sed 's|.*github.com[:/]||' | sed 's|\.git$||')
19:```
20:

22:
23:## Epic Sync — Push Epic + Tasks to GitHub
24:
25:**Trigger**: User wants to push a local epic and its tasks to GitHub as issues.
26:
27:### Preflight
28:- Verify `.claude/epics/<name>/epic.md` exists.
29:- Verify numbered task files exist — if none: "❌ No tasks to sync. Decompose the epic first."
30:
31:### Process
32:
33:**Step 1 — Create epic issue:**
34:
35:Strip frontmatter from epic.md, then:
36:```bash
37:sed '1,/^---$/d; 1,/^---$/d' .claude/epics/<name>/epic.md > /tmp/epic-body.md
38:epic_number=$(gh issue create \
39:  --repo "$REPO" \
40:  --title "Epic: <name>" \
41:  --body-file /tmp/epic-body.md \
42:  --label "epic,epic:<name>,feature" \
43:  --json number -q .number)
44:```
45:
46:**Step 2 — Create task sub-issues:**
47:
48:Check if `gh-sub-issue` extension is available:
49:```bash
50:if gh extension list | grep -q "yahsan2/gh-sub-issue"; then
51:  use_subissues=true
52:fi
53:```
54:
55:For <5 tasks: create sequentially.
56:For ≥5 tasks: use parallel Task agents (3-4 tasks per batch).
57:
58:Per task:
59:```bash
60:sed '1,/^---$/d; 1,/^---$/d' <task_file> > /tmp/task-body.md
61:task_number=$(gh issue create \
62:  --repo "$REPO" \
63:  --title "<task_name>" \
64:  --body-file /tmp/task-body.md \
65:  --label "task,epic:<name>" \
66:  --json number -q .number)
67:# or with sub-issues:
68:# gh sub-issue create --parent $epic_number ...
69:```
70:
71:**Step 3 — Rename task files and update references:**
72:
73:After all issues are created, rename `001.md` → `<issue_number>.md` and update all `depends_on`/`conflicts_with` arrays to use real issue numbers (not sequential numbers).
74:
75:```bash
76:# Build old→new mapping, then for each task file:
77:sed -i.bak "s/\b001\b/<new_num_1>/g" <file>  # repeat for each mapping
78:mv 001.md <new_num>.md
79:```
80:
81:**Step 4 — Update frontmatter:**
82:```bash
83:current_date=$(date -u +"%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ")
84:# Update github: and updated: fields in epic.md and each task file
85:github_url="https://github.com/$REPO/issues/<number>"
86:sed -i.bak "/^github:/c\\github: $github_url" <file>
87:sed -i.bak "/^updated:/c\\updated: $current_date" <file>
88:rm <file>.bak
89:```
90:
91:**Step 5 — Create worktree for the epic:**
92:```bash
93:git checkout main && git pull origin main
94:git worktree add ../epic-<name> -b epic/<name>
95:```
96:
97:**Step 6 — Create github-mapping.md:**
98:```markdown
99:# GitHub Issue Mapping
100:Epic: #<N> - https://github.com/<repo>/issues/<N>
101:Tasks:
102:- #<N>: <title> - https://github.com/<repo>/issues/<N>
103:Synced: <datetime>
104:```
105:
106:**Output:**
107:```

113:```

117:## Issue Sync — Post Progress to GitHub
118:
119:**Trigger**: User wants to sync local development progress to a GitHub issue as a comment.
120:
121:### Preflight
122:- Verify issue exists: `gh issue view <N> --json state`
123:- Check `.claude/epics/*/updates/<N>/` exists with a `progress.md` file.
124:- Check `last_sync` in progress.md — if synced <5 minutes ago, confirm before proceeding.
125:
126:### Process
127:
128:Gather updates from `.claude/epics/<epic>/updates/<N>/` (progress.md, notes.md, commits.md).
129:
130:Format and post a comment:
131:```bash
132:gh issue comment <N> --body-file /tmp/update-comment.md
133:```
134:
135:Comment format:
136:```markdown
137:## 🔄 Progress Update - <date>
138:
139:### ✅ Completed Work
140:### 🔄 In Progress
141:### 📝 Technical Notes
142:### 📊 Acceptance Criteria Status
143:### 🚀 Next Steps
144:### ⚠️ Blockers
145:
146:---

148:```
149:
150:After posting: update `last_sync` in progress.md frontmatter, update `updated` in the task file.
151:

159:## Closing an Issue
160:
161:**Trigger**: User marks a task complete.
162:
163:### Process
164:
165:1. Find the local task file (`.claude/epics/*/<N>.md`).
166:2. Update frontmatter: `status: closed`, `updated: <now>`.
167:3. Post completion comment:
168:```bash
169:echo "✅ Task completed — all acceptance criteria met." | gh issue comment <N> --body-file -
170:gh issue close <N>
171:```
172:4. Check off the task in the epic issue body:
173:```bash
174:gh issue view <epic_N> --json body -q .body > /tmp/epic-body.md
175:sed -i "s/- \[ \] #<N>/- [x] #<N>/" /tmp/epic-body.md
176:gh issue edit <epic_N> --body-file /tmp/epic-body.md
177:```
178:5. Recalculate and update epic progress: `progress = closed_tasks / total_tasks * 100`
179:
180:---
181:
182:## Merging an Epic
183:
184:**Trigger**: User wants to merge a completed epic back to main.
185:
186:### Preflight
187:- Verify worktree `../epic-<name>` exists.
188:- Check for uncommitted changes in the worktree — block if dirty.
189:- Warn if any task issues are still open.
190:
191:### Process
192:
193:```bash
194:# From worktree: run project tests if detectable
195:cd ../epic-<name>
196:# detect and run: npm test / pytest / cargo test / go test / etc.
197:
198:# From main repo:
199:git checkout main && git pull origin main
200:git merge epic/<name> --no-ff -m "Merge epic: <name>"
201:git push origin main
202:
203:# Cleanup
204:git worktree remove ../epic-<name>
205:git branch -d epic/<name>
206:git push origin --delete epic/<name>
207:
208:# Archive
209:mkdir -p .claude/epics/archived/
210:mv .claude/epics/<name> .claude/epics/archived/
211:
212:# Close GitHub issues
213:epic_issue=$(grep 'github:' .claude/epics/archived/<name>/epic.md | grep -oE '[0-9]+$')

216:
217:Update epic.md frontmatter: `status: completed`.
218:
219:---
220:
221:## Reporting a Bug Against a Completed Issue
222:
223:**Trigger**: User finds a bug while testing a completed or in-progress issue — e.g. "found a bug in issue 42", "email validation is broken, came up while testing issue 42".
224:
225:The workflow should stay automated: create a linked bug task without losing context from the original issue.
226:
227:### Process
228:
229:**Step 1 — Read the original issue for context:**
230:```bash
231:gh issue view <original_N> --json title,body,labels
232:```
233:Also read the local task file if it exists: `.claude/epics/*/<original_N>.md`
234:
235:**Step 2 — Create a local bug task file:**
236:
237:```markdown
238:---
239:name: Bug: <short description>
240:status: open
241:created: <run: date -u +"%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ">
242:updated: <same>
243:github: (will be set on sync)
244:depends_on: []
245:parallel: false
246:conflicts_with: []
247:bug_for: <original_N>
248:---
249:
250:# Bug: <short description>
251:
252:## Context
253:Found while working on / testing issue #<original_N>: <original title>
254:
255:## Description
256:<what's broken>
257:
258:## Steps to Reproduce
259:<steps>
260:
261:## Expected vs Actual
262:- Expected: 
263:- Actual: 
264:
265:## Acceptance Criteria
266:- [ ] Bug is fixed
267:- [ ] Original issue #<original_N> behaviour is unaffected
268:
269:## Effort Estimate
270:- Size: XS/S
271:```
272:
273:Save to `.claude/epics/<same_epic_as_original>/bug-<original_N>-<slug>.md`
274:
275:**Step 3 — Create a linked GitHub issue:**
276:```bash
277:gh issue create \
278:  --repo "$REPO" \
279:  --title "Bug: <short description>" \
280:  --body "$(cat /tmp/bug-body.md)" \
281:  --label "bug,epic:<epic_name>" \
282:  --json number -q .number
283:```
284:
285:The issue body should open with `Fixes / follow-up to #<original_N>` so GitHub auto-links them.
286:
287:**Step 4 — Update the local file** with the GitHub issue number and rename to `<new_N>.md`.
288:
289:**Output:**
290:```
291:✅ Bug issue created: #<new_N> — "Bug: <short description>"
292:  Linked to: #<original_N>
293:  Epic: <epic_name>
294:
295:Start fixing it: "start working on issue <new_N>"
296:```

Z:\claude-sota\.claude\rules\convergence-gate.md:118:## Anti-pattern: Row-2 fabrication-test FAIL
Z:\claude-sota\.claude\rules\convergence-gate.md:120:When running the 5-row bar's Row 2 (Numeric — measurable improvement), a README presenting **≥3 numeric performance claims without methodology citation** (no repro script link, no benchmark repo, no dataset name) is **auto-FAIL** — do not attempt live A/B to verify, just REJECT. This short-circuits the primary-source rule: vendor marketing numbers that aren't backed by a reproducible artifact are false-by-default until proven otherwise.
Z:\claude-sota\.claude\rules\convergence-gate.md:125:3. If ≥3 claims lack citations, Row-2 auto-FAIL → REJECT verdict bypasses expensive verification step
Z:\claude-sota\.claude\rules\convergence-gate.md:129:**Why auto-FAIL not just downgrade**: across multiple prior live A/B verifications of fabrication-pattern candidates, none survived verification. The prior probability of "≥3 unsourced claims yet verifiable" is empirically near-zero. Running the bench is budget-wasting ritual.

25:# KISS / DRY / YAGNI
26:
29:# Reference: .claude/rules/canonical.md Must Never #9 "Write speculative helpers/abstractions" (sister cardinal-rule body — this file is the operational instantiation)
30:# Reference: .claude/rules/karpathy-adapted.md §2 "Simplicity First" (sister-rule operational instantiation; Karpathy P2 → KISS/DRY/YAGNI is the implementation)
34:
35:Three non-negotiable shipping principles.
36:
37:## Keep It Simple (KISS)
38:
39:Prefer the simplest solution that actually works. Optimize for clarity, not cleverness. No premature optimization.
40:
41:## Don't Repeat Yourself (DRY)
42:
43:Extract repeated logic only when repetition is *real*, not speculative. Three similar lines is better than a premature abstraction (per root `CLAUDE.md` hard rule).
44:
45:## You Aren't Gonna Need It (YAGNI)
46:
47:Do not build features, flags, or abstractions before they are needed. No "future-proofing" shims, no backwards-compat layers for unreleased APIs.
48:
49:## Why
50:
52:
54:
55:## How to apply
56:
57:- Before extracting a helper: grep for the duplication. If <3 call sites, inline it.
59:- Before a new abstraction layer: write the concrete path first, refactor only when a second caller actually arrives.
60:- Before a "nice to have" feature in a bug-fix PR: split it out. Bug fixes don't need surrounding cleanup.
61:- Post-change audit: run `grep -r "<new_symbol>"` — if only the definition site matches, you just wrote dead code.
62:
63:## Related rules
64:
65:- `karpathy-adapted.md` §2 — Karpathy P2 Simplicity First; this rule is the operational instantiation
66:- `canonical.md` Must Never #9 — cardinal hard-rule statement; this file ships the enforceable body
67:- `citation-discipline.md` — sister cardinal-rule body (cite-format contract); both are foundational discipline files
68:- `port-note-discipline.md` — when porting, do NOT speculatively add features beyond what parent had (YAGNI applied to the port itself)
69:- `evidence-policy.md` Stuck Detection — "Do not invent APIs" is YAGNI applied to API design

82:## How to apply
83:
84:**Decision tree** before spawning multi-agent work:
85:
86:1. **Decomposable into N independent sub-tasks?** (each agent's output doesn't depend on another's)
87:   - YES → parallel-wave (this rule)
88:   - NO → serial chain (Agent → next Agent with output as input)
89:
90:2. **Independent sub-tasks count?**
91:   - 1: single Agent() call
92:   - 2-3: parallel-wave (low overhead, fast convergence)
93:   - 4-6: parallel-wave sweet spot (per cycle-436 6-agent + cycle-c0cd0eac 7-agent evidence)
94:   - 7+: requires explicit shard contract + non-overlapping scopes + budget cap + synthesis plan (see `team-orchestration.md` (LOCAL — sister-port iter-#5) §Team-Lifecycle Hygiene)
95:   - 10-20: use the swarm/migration recipe in `parallel-sessions.md` (LOCAL — ported iter-12; NOT this rule)
96:
98:   - **MUST** use single parent message with multiple Agent tool-use content blocks for true parallelism
99:   - **MUST NOT** chain Agent() calls in separate messages (each message round-trips)
100:   - Each agent brief MUST be self-contained (no visibility into other agents' work)
102:
103:**Brief discipline**:
104:- Each agent gets independent scope + verification protocol
105:- Synthesis agent (if needed) runs SERIAL after parallel wave (consumes all parallel outputs)
106:- Critic agent (Eve-pattern) runs SERIAL after synthesis (pressure-tests synthesis verdict)

108:## Wave shape patterns (non-exhaustive)

110:For the full taxonomy, defer to `team-orchestration.md` (LOCAL — sister-port iter-#5); this section is the empirically-grounded subset specific to this rule's evidence ladder:
111:
112:- **Research wave**: N agents probe N independent SOTA sources in parallel → synthesis agent merges (cycle-245 `265c31b9`, cycle-255 `ed3abedb`)
113:- **Audit wave**: N agents audit N independent codebase axes in parallel → synthesis with verdict (cycle-441 `86f595ed`, cycle-c0cd0eac)
114:- **Cross-model wave**: 1 Claude agent + 1 codex T1 fire concurrent (different model architectures probe different surfaces) → convergence check (iter-10 of this arc)

116:- **Split-responsibility proposal wave**: read-only agents inspect/propose, parent applies mechanically (cycle-356 `c8f47a4c`)
117:- **Disjoint implementation/port wave**: agents own separate file/module scopes, parent synthesizes and verifies (`f49eba1`, `b333051`)

153:## Anti-patterns
154:
155:- **Serial chain when parallel-decomposable**: each Agent() spawn round-trips ~30-60s; serializing 4 independent tasks costs ~2-4 min vs ~30-60s parallel wave (4-6× overhead).
156:- **Parallel chain with hidden dependencies**: if Agent B needs Agent A's output, parallel wave produces incoherent merge; revert to serial.
160:- **Overlapping write scopes without isolation**: per `parallel-sessions.md` (LOCAL — ported iter-12), read-only agents may run concurrently while state-modifying agents must serialize OR isolate (worktree per agent).

# Conventions — File Formats, Paths & Rules

Read this before doing any file operations across all phases.

---

## Directory Structure

```
.claude/
├── prds/
│   └── <feature-name>.md          # Product requirement documents
├── epics/
│   ├── <feature-name>/
│   │   ├── epic.md                # Technical epic
│   │   ├── <N>.md                 # Task files (named by GitHub issue number after sync)
│   │   ├── <N>-analysis.md        # Parallel work stream analysis
│   │   ├── github-mapping.md      # Issue number → URL mapping
│   │   ├── execution-status.md    # Active agents tracker
│   │   └── updates/
│   │       └── <issue_N>/
│   │           ├── stream-A.md    # Per-agent progress
│   │           ├── progress.md    # Overall issue progress
│   │           └── execution.md  # Execution state
│   └── archived/
│       └── <feature-name>/        # Completed epics
└── context/                       # Project context docs (separate system)
```

---

## Frontmatter Schemas

### PRD (.claude/prds/<name>.md)
```yaml
---
name: <feature-name>        # kebab-case, matches filename
description: <one-liner>    # used in lists and summaries
status: backlog | active | completed
created: <ISO 8601>         # date -u +"%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ"
---
```

### Epic (.claude/epics/<name>/epic.md)
```yaml
---
name: <feature-name>
status: backlog | in-progress | completed
created: <ISO 8601>
updated: <ISO 8601>
progress: 0%                # recalculated when tasks close
prd: .claude/prds/<name>.md
github: https://github.com/<owner>/<repo>/issues/<N>  # set on sync
---
```

### Task (.claude/epics/<name>/<N>.md)
```yaml
---
name: <Task Title>
status: open | in-progress | closed
created: <ISO 8601>
updated: <ISO 8601>
github: https://github.com/<owner>/<repo>/issues/<N>  # set on sync
depends_on: []              # issue numbers this must wait for
parallel: true              # can run concurrently with non-conflicting tasks
conflicts_with: []          # issue numbers that touch the same files
---
```

### Progress (.claude/epics/<name>/updates/<N>/progress.md)
```yaml
---
issue: <N>
started: <ISO 8601>
last_sync: <ISO 8601>
completion: 0%
---
```

---

## Datetime Rule

Always get real current datetime from the system — never use placeholder text:
```bash
date -u +"%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ"
```

---

## Frontmatter Update Pattern

When updating a single frontmatter field in an existing file:
```bash
sed -i.bak "/^<field>:/c\\<field>: <value>" <file>
rm <file>.bak
```

When stripping frontmatter to get body content for GitHub:
```bash
sed '1,/^---$/d; 1,/^---$/d' <file> > /tmp/body.md
```

---

## GitHub Operations

### Repository Safety Check (run before any write operation)
```bash
remote_url=$(git remote get-url origin 2>/dev/null || echo "")
if [[ "$remote_url" == *"automazeio/ccpm"* ]]; then
  echo "❌ Cannot write to the CCPM template repository."
  echo "Update remote: git remote set-url origin https://github.com/YOUR/REPO.git"
  exit 1
fi
REPO=$(echo "$remote_url" | sed 's|.*github.com[:/]||' | sed 's|\.git$||')
```

### Authentication
Don't pre-check authentication. Run the `gh` command and handle failure:
```bash
gh <command> || echo "❌ GitHub CLI failed. Run: gh auth login"
```

### Getting Issue Numbers
```bash
# From a task file's github field:
grep 'github:' <file> | grep -oE '[0-9]+$'
```

---

## Git / Worktree Conventions

- One branch per epic: `epic/<name>`
- Worktrees live at `../epic-<name>/` (sibling to project root)
- Always start branches from an up-to-date main:
  ```bash
  git checkout main && git pull origin main
  git worktree add ../epic-<name> -b epic/<name>
  ```
- Commit format inside epics: `Issue #<N>: <description>`
- Never use `--force` in any git operation

---

## Naming Conventions

- Feature names: kebab-case, lowercase, letters/numbers/hyphens, starts with a letter
- Task files before sync: `001.md`, `002.md`, ... (sequential)
- Task files after sync: renamed to GitHub issue number (e.g., `1234.md`)
- Labels applied on sync: `epic`, `epic:<name>`, `feature` (for epics); `task`, `epic:<name>` (for tasks)

---

## Epic Progress Calculation

```bash
total=$(ls .claude/epics/<name>/[0-9]*.md 2>/dev/null | wc -l)
closed=$(grep -l '^status: closed' .claude/epics/<name>/[0-9]*.md 2>/dev/null | wc -l)
progress=$((closed * 100 / total))
```

Update epic frontmatter when any task closes.

If the candidate proposes adopting a primitive (MCP / skill / library / tool) that is structurally sound (Probes 1-6 PASS): verify the **harness-side operational driver** BEFORE adoption. Probe 7 splits into two outcomes — `.a` REJECT (demand-absence) and `.b` STUDY-PILOT eligible (demand-creates-new-workflow). The split closes the Wave 27 catch-22 surfaced at `tmp/wave27-agentE-saturation-adversarial-2026-05-05.md:46-56,89-106` (Probe 7.a as currently worded auto-REJECTs any primitive that creates a NEW workflow because no sss invocation surface yet exists — circular per Jeffries YAGNI canonical statement at `kiss-dry-yagni.md:31-33`).

**Hard precondition (before applying .a or .b)**: earlier Axis-4 blockers WIN. If the candidate duplicates an existing shipped primitive (Probe 4 plugin-namespace), collides with plugin namespace, requires an unmet harness/mode assumption (Probe 5 mode-harness-shape), fails Probe 6 (license/registry/build-deps blocker), is SUPERSEDED-BY-X (existing primitive owns the workflow), or is a META-HARNESS competing-framework shape per `docs/verified-avoid.md` Cohort 1, classify under that blocker instead. Probe 7.b is ONLY available for structurally sound primitives that create a genuinely new, non-duplicative workflow.

#### Probe 7.a — DEMAND-ABSENCE (REJECT-FOR-FIT)

What sss workflow / invocation surface / consumer would route through this primitive TODAY? Verify the 3-clause check:
- Cite a specific path (existing or queued)
- Is the candidate's value proposition met by an EXISTING shipped primitive? (e.g., "graphiti MCP already provides FalkorDB temporal KG access" → dbhub adds no marginal value AS A REPLACEMENT)
- Is the candidate displacing or extending? Displacement requires migration plan; extension requires marginal-value evidence

If NO current/queued workflow AND .b 5-clause check (below) does not survive, REJECT-FOR-FIT.a (demand-absence) — REJECT-decisive.

#### Probe 7.b — DEMAND-CREATES-NEW-WORKFLOW (STUDY-PILOT eligible)

A structurally sound primitive may create a genuinely new workflow that no existing sss primitive serves. STUDY-PILOT eligibility requires ALL 5 clauses to hold (codex T1 NEEDS-REVISION conf=0.84 Q2 prescription at `.claude/state/codex_consult_ship27_3_probe7_demand_creates_OUT.txt`):

1. **Named operational use case**: cite the query/workflow and the consumer that would exercise it
2. **Cited local input/source path**: identify the concrete data, repo path, tool surface, or state file (e.g., `Z:/claude-sota/.claude/state/mcp_overhead_audit.jsonl`)
3. **Wiring path**: name the adapter/ETL/config needed to make the primitive consume the source; if wiring is non-trivial, it is part of the pilot cost
4. **Incumbent comparison**: explain why existing shipped primitives or simpler local commands (`rg`, `jq`, GitNexus, Langfuse MCP, graphiti, mcp-memory, one-off Python scripts) do not already satisfy the use case OR are materially worse
5. **Reversible time-box**: define owner, max pilot cost, 30-day success criterion, and retirement path

**Pilot failure**: retire to `disabledMcpjsonServers` if applicable and document in `docs/verified-avoid.md` under the matching failure cohort; create a dedicated retired-pilot / demand-not-realized cohort only after n>=2 same-shape recurrences. NOTE: `verified-avoid.md` Cohort 2 is specifically Probe 6 direct-file/registry blockers per `docs/verified-avoid.md:47-49`; failed demand-pilots do NOT belong there by default. # Structure — Break Down an Epic

This phase converts a technical epic into concrete, numbered task files with dependency and parallelization metadata.

---

## Epic Decomposition

**Trigger**: User wants to break an epic into actionable tasks.

### Preflight
- Verify `.claude/epics/<name>/epic.md` exists with valid frontmatter.
- If numbered task files (001.md, 002.md...) already exist in the epic directory, list them and confirm deletion before recreating.
- If epic status is "completed", warn the user before proceeding.

### Process

Read the epic fully. Analyze for parallelism — which pieces of work can happen simultaneously without file conflicts?

**Task types to consider:**
- Setup: environment, scaffolding, dependencies
- Data: models, schemas, migrations
- API: endpoints, services, integration
- UI: components, pages, styling
- Tests: unit, integration, e2e
- Docs: README, API docs, changelogs

**Parallelization strategy by epic size:**
- Small (<5 tasks): create sequentially
- Medium (5–10 tasks): batch into 2–3 groups, spawn parallel Task agents
- Large (>10 tasks): analyze dependencies first, launch parallel agents (max 5 concurrent), create dependent tasks after prerequisites

For parallel creation, use the Task tool:
```yaml
Task:
  description: "Create task files batch N"
  subagent_type: "general-purpose"
  prompt: |
    Create task files for epic: <name>
    Tasks to create: [list 3-4 tasks]
    Save to: .claude/epics/<name>/001.md, 002.md, etc.
    Follow the task file format exactly.
    Return: list of files created.
```

### Task File Format

```markdown
---
name: <Task Title>
status: open
created: <run: date -u +"%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ">
updated: <same as created>
github: (will be set on sync)
depends_on: []
parallel: true
conflicts_with: []
---

# Task: <Task Title>

## Description

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ]

## Technical Details

## Dependencies

## Effort Estimate
- Size: XS/S/M/L/XL
- Hours: N

## Definition of Done
- [ ] Code implemented
- [ ] Tests written and passing
- [ ] Code reviewed
```

**Numbering**: sequential 001.md, 002.md, etc. Tasks are renamed to GitHub issue numbers after sync — do not hard-code dependencies by filename, use the `depends_on` array.

### After Creating All Tasks

Append a summary to the epic file:

```markdown
## Tasks Created
- [ ] 001.md - <Title> (parallel: true/false)
- [ ] 002.md - <Title> (parallel: true/false)

Total tasks: N
Parallel tasks: N
Sequential tasks: N
Estimated total effort: N hours
```

**After completion**: Confirm "✅ Created N tasks for epic: <name>" and suggest: "Ready to push to GitHub? Say: sync the <name> epic"

---

## Dependency Rules
- `depends_on` lists task numbers that must complete before this task can start.
- `parallel: true` means the task can run concurrently with others it doesn't conflict with.
- `conflicts_with` lists tasks that touch the same files — these cannot run in parallel.
- Circular dependencies are an error — check before finalizing.

# Plan — Capture Requirements

This phase turns an idea into a structured PRD, then converts the PRD into a technical epic ready for decomposition.

---

## Writing a PRD

**Trigger**: User wants to plan a new feature, product requirement, or area of work.

### Preflight
- Check if `.claude/prds/<name>.md` already exists — if so, confirm overwrite before proceeding.
- Ensure `.claude/prds/` directory exists; create it if not.
- Feature name must be kebab-case (lowercase, letters/numbers/hyphens, starts with a letter). If not: "❌ Feature name must be kebab-case. Example: user-auth, payment-v2"

### Process

Conduct a genuine brainstorming session before writing anything. Ask the user:
- What problem does this solve?
- Who are the users affected?
- What does success look like?
- What's explicitly out of scope?
- What are the constraints (tech, time, resources)?

Then write `.claude/prds/<name>.md` with this frontmatter and structure:

```markdown
---
name: <feature-name>
description: <one-line summary>
status: backlog
created: <run: date -u +"%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ">
---

# PRD: <feature-name>

## Executive Summary
## Problem Statement
## User Stories
## Functional Requirements
## Non-Functional Requirements
## Success Criteria
## Constraints & Assumptions
## Out of Scope
## Dependencies
```

**Quality gates before saving:**
- No placeholder text in any section
- User stories include acceptance criteria
- Success criteria are measurable
- Out of scope is explicitly listed

**After creation**: Confirm "✅ PRD created: `.claude/prds/<name>.md`" and suggest: "Ready to create technical epic? Say: parse the <name> PRD"

---

## Parsing a PRD into a Technical Epic

**Trigger**: User wants to convert an existing PRD into a technical implementation plan.

### Preflight
- Verify `.claude/prds/<name>.md` exists with valid frontmatter (name, description, status, created).
- Check if `.claude/epics/<name>/epic.md` already exists — confirm overwrite if so.

### Process

Read the PRD fully, then produce `.claude/epics/<name>/epic.md`:

```markdown
---
name: <feature-name>
status: backlog
created: <run: date -u +"%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ">
progress: 0%
prd: .claude/prds/<name>.md
github: (will be set on sync)
---

# Epic: <feature-name>

## Overview
## Architecture Decisions
## Technical Approach
### Frontend Components
### Backend Services
### Infrastructure
## Implementation Strategy
## Task Breakdown Preview
## Dependencies
## Success Criteria (Technical)
## Estimated Effort
```

**Key constraints:**
- Aim for ≤10 tasks total — prefer simplicity over completeness.
- Look for ways to leverage existing functionality before creating new code.
- Identify parallelization opportunities in the task breakdown preview.

**After creation**: Confirm "✅ Epic created: `.claude/epics/<name>/epic.md`" and suggest: "Ready to decompose into tasks? Say: decompose the <name> epic"

---

## Editing a PRD or Epic

Read the file first, make targeted edits preserving all frontmatter. Update the `updated` frontmatter field with current datetime.

## The rule

Sota-researcher / architect / general agent dispatches that surface SOTA candidates MUST include a **harness-fit verification step** asking "is this applicable to OUR specific architecture?" — beyond the convergence-gate Axis 1+2+3 (T1 sources / T2 practitioners / Axis 3 stability) that scores SOTA-status. Without harness-fit, candidates pass convergence-gate AND still fail at ship-target verification because of architectural mismatch invisible to upstream-source-only audit.

This is **convergence-gate Axis 4** (harness-fit) — separate from Axis 1+2+3 (which classify SOTA-status of the candidate ITSELF) and applied AFTER convergence-gate PASS, BEFORE ship-target verification.

## When this rule applies

Whenever an agent (sota-researcher / architect / general-purpose / Explore / code-reviewer / debugger) returns a ship-candidate ranking from a Wave-N dispatch:

1. The agent's convergence-gate verdict is necessary BUT NOT SUFFICIENT for ship-readiness
2. The candidate may be valid SOTA AND inapplicable to claude-sota
3. Apply the 4-axis harness-fit probe BEFORE writing T1 consult prompt OR queuing the ship

## How to apply (4-axis probe)

Before declaring an agent's ship-candidate "ready":

### Probe 1 — count-OVER

If the candidate claims a count delta (commit count, file count, line count, star count): verify against authoritative local source (`git log`, `wc -l`, `Glob | wc -l`, `mcp__github__search_repositories` star refresh) BEFORE accepting. Agent counts via remote APIs can drift, paginate-truncate, or include stale cache.

### Probe 2 — SDK-vs-CLI surface

If the candidate proposes adopting an SDK feature / config flag / env var: verify the **invocation surface** exists in claude-sota:
- Does claude-sota use the SDK or CLI? Check `.claude/hooks/scripts/*.py` + `.claude/settings.json` env block
- Does the candidate's mechanism map to claude-sota's actual mode (interactive vs print-mode vs SDK-managed-agent)?
- If the candidate requires a mode claude-sota doesn't run in, REJECT-for-fit even if SOTA-valid upstream

### Probe 3 — architectural-API

If the candidate proposes a primitive (cache_control, prompt-cache, structured-outputs, batch-API): verify the **API ecosystem match**:
- Anthropic-API primitive vs OpenAI-API primitive vs vendor-neutral OTel
- claude-sota's gpt5.5/codex hooks talk to OpenAI-API endpoints; Anthropic-only primitives don't apply there
- Cross-check before assuming "this Anthropic pattern works on codex"

### Probe 5 — mode-harness-shape

If the candidate proposes adopting a skill/workflow/pattern with operational mode dependencies (HARD-GATE on user interaction, interactive-vs-autonomous mismatch, meta-skill assumptions about sister-harness presence, file-count or size-sprawl orthogonal to existing layout): verify the **operational mode + harness shape match**:
- Does the candidate skill HARD-GATE on interactive user approval? Verify against claude-sota's autonomous /loop mode (incompatible)

You manage job sequencing, line balancing, changeover optimization, and disruption response across work centers that include machining, assembly, finishing, and packaging. Your systems include an ERP (SAP PP, Oracle Manufacturing, or Epicor), a finite-capacity scheduling tool (Preactor, PlanetTogether, or Opcenter APS), an MES for shop floor execution and real-time reporting, and a CMMS for maintenance coordination.
